lead: A fibre-reinforced plastic (FRP) carries load along stiff fibres held in a weak polymer matrix. One thin layer, a ply, is stiff along the fibres and soft across them. Such a material is orthotropic and needs four constants. Aircraft wing skins and spacecraft panels use FRP because a tailored ply sequence puts stiffness where the load needs it. This chapter builds the plane-stress stiffness matrix of one ply, along its fibres and rotated to structure axes.
prereq: You need stress, strain, E and ν from Unit 1, and plane stress from 6.1.

sections.h3: Fibre, matrix and the orthotropic ply

blocks.text: An FRP is a polymer matrix, usually epoxy, holding long thin fibres of carbon, glass or aramid. The fibres are stiff and strong along their length. The matrix is weak but tough: it separates the fibres, transfers load by shear and seals out moisture.

One layer is a ply, or lamina, often about 0.125 mm thick for carbon/epoxy. Axis 1 runs along the fibres, axis 2 across them in the plane, axis 3 through the thickness. A wing-skin ply is in plane stress (σ3 = 0), so only axes 1 and 2 matter.

The fibres lie in one direction, so stiffness along 1 is far higher than along 2. The material has three symmetry planes and is orthotropic. Four constants describe it: E1 along the fibres, E2 across, ν12 (contraction in 2 per unit strain in 1) and G12 (in-plane shear modulus).
Carbon/epoxy typically has E1 = 140 GPa, E2 = 10 GPa, ν12 = 0.30 and G12 = 5 GPa; glass/epoxy near E1 = 40 GPa, E2 = 8 GPa. G12 is low in both because the matrix carries shear.

sections.h3: The four constants and the Q matrix

blocks.text: Hooke's law for one ply, in its own 1–2 axes, uses a 3 × 3 stiffness matrix Q:

blocks.where: σ1, σ2 are normal stresses (Pa) along and across the fibres; τ12 is the in-plane shear stress (Pa); ε1, ε2 are normal strains and γ12 is the engineering shear strain (all dimensionless).
the Q's are reduced stiffnesses (Pa); ν21 = ν12E2/E1 is the second Poisson ratio, dimensionless. All moduli in the same unit, normally GPa.

blocks.text: The denominator appears because the two Poisson effects act together. In a free uniaxial test the ply contracts sideways, which lowers the stress for a given ε1, so the measured E1 is slightly smaller than Q11. Q11 is the stiffness when that sideways contraction is blocked.
Symmetry of Q requires ν12/E1 = ν21/E2, so ν21 = ν12E2/E1, always much smaller than ν12.

Do not call Q11 a modulus. E1 and E2 come from a uniaxial test where the ply contracts freely sideways. Q11, Q12 and Q22 come from the state where sideways contraction is fully prevented (ε2 = 0). That is why Q11 is slightly larger than E1. The word reduced refers to setting the through-thickness stress to zero (σ3 = 0).

sections.h3: Rotating the ply to laminate axes

blocks.text: In a real panel the plies are laid at angles. Take structure axes x–y and let θ be the angle from x to the fibre axis 1, counter-clockwise positive. Write m = cos θ and n = sin θ. The stiffness in x–y is Qbar:
Qbar11 = Q11 m⁴ + 2(Q12 + 2Q66) m²n² + Q22 n⁴
blocks.where: Qbar11 is the stiffness along x (Pa); θ is the ply angle in radians; m = cos θ, n = sin θ. Qbar22 follows by swapping m and n; Qbar12 and Qbar66 have similar standard forms.

blocks.text: Two new terms appear, Qbar16 and Qbar26. They are zero at 0° and 90° and reach their largest values at intermediate angles, near 30° for Qbar16 and near 60° for Qbar26 in a typical carbon/epoxy ply; at 45° both are appreciable. They are extension–shear coupling: pull a 45° ply along x and it also shears. At θ = 0°, Qbar equals Q. At θ = 90°, Qbar11 becomes Q22.

This is how composites are tailored: ±45° plies add shear stiffness, 0° plies axial stiffness, 90° plies transverse and hoop stiffness. Unbalanced coupling gives bend–twist coupling for aeroelastic tailoring. Stacking plies through the thickness comes next in 6.8.

examples.question: A carbon/epoxy ply has E1 = 140 GPa, E2 = 10 GPa, ν12 = 0.30 and G12 = 5 GPa. Find ν21, the factor (1 − ν12ν21), and Q11, Q22, Q12 and Q66.
examples.check:
E1 = 140.0
E2 = 10.0
nu12 = 0.30
G12 = 5.0
nu21 = nu12 * E2 / E1
den = 1 - nu12 * nu21
Q11 = E1 / den
Q22 = E2 / den
Q12 = nu12 * E2 / den
Q66 = G12
print(round(nu21, 4))
print(round(den, 4))
print(round(Q11, 2))
print(round(Q22, 2))
print(round(Q12, 2))
print(round(Q66, 2))

traps: Using Q11 = E1 directly and dropping (1 − ν12ν21); the error is about 0.6% here, but grows to roughly 1.4% for glass/epoxy because E2/E1 is about 0.2 instead of 0.07, making ν12ν21 four times bigger.
Mixing up ν12 and ν21. Only ν12 is measured; ν21 = ν12E2/E1 is always the smaller number.
Feeding degrees into sin and cos in a program. The transformation needs radians; convert with θ × π/180 first.
Writing Q12 = ν12E1/den. The correct numerator is ν12E2, so Q12 stays close to 3 GPa, not 42 GPa.
Believing Qbar16 and Qbar26 are always zero. They vanish only at 0° and 90°; at other angles they couple extension and shear.

quiz.q: Define an orthotropic lamina and name its principal axes.
quiz.a: A thin layer with three mutually perpendicular planes of material symmetry. Axis 1 is along the fibres, axis 2 across them in the plane, axis 3 through the thickness.

quiz.q: Why is E2 much lower than E1 in a carbon/epoxy ply?
quiz.a: Along axis 1 the stiff fibres carry almost all the load. Across axis 2 the load passes through the soft matrix between fibres, so stiffness is matrix-dominated and roughly ten times lower.

quiz.q: State the relation between ν12 and ν21 and explain why it is needed.
quiz.a: ν12/E1 = ν21/E2, so ν21 = ν12E2/E1. It keeps the Q matrix symmetric and lets one measured Poisson ratio give the other.

quiz.q: A glass/epoxy ply has E1 = 40 GPa, E2 = 8 GPa, ν12 = 0.26, G12 = 4 GPa. Find ν21, the factor (1 − ν12ν21) and Q11.
A single ply is loaded along x at 45° to the fibres and a shear strain appears. Explain.
quiz.a: At θ = 45° the terms Qbar16 and Qbar26 are non-zero, so normal stress produces shear strain. The fibres and matrix deform in a scissors pattern because the load is not aligned with either principal direction.

quiz.q: What happens to Qbar when θ = 90°, and why is such a ply still useful?
quiz.a: Qbar11 becomes Q22 and Qbar22 becomes Q11, because axes 1 and 2 have swapped relative to x and y. The ply is soft along the main load but stiff across it, so it controls transverse and hoop stresses and matrix cracking in a laminate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Micro-mechanics predicts E1, E2 and G12 from fibre volume fraction by rule of mixtures, so a ply can be designed before it is made. Failure of composites is handled by Tsai–Hill or Tsai–Wu criteria rather than a single yield stress, because fibre tension, matrix tension and shear fail at different loads. Industry builds large integrated structures by automated fibre placement, and newer curricula add thermoplastic composites that can be welded instead of bonded. Search next for micromechanics, Tsai–Wu, cure residual stress and barely visible impact damage.
